We are developing an educational game designed to help children learn and serve as a valuable learning tool in classrooms.
summary:
Delta-V Dilemma is an educational space mission design game where players build spacecraft, manage budgets, and solve engineering challenges. Players choose from 63 components, balancing mass, propulsion, power, communications, and scientific instruments to meet each mission’s requirements.

The game includes individual challenges, a multi-mission Story Mode, and NASA missions featuring real asteroid targets. It integrates three datasets: NHATS for asteroid mission dates and delta‑V requirements, JPL Horizons for solar distances, and SORCE for sunlight measurements used in solar-power calculations.

Interactive explanations, component illustrations, and flight reports help players understand why their designs succeed or fail. The game combines real scientific data with simplified engineering and clearly labeled cost estimates, making spacecraft design approachable through experimentation.
details:
Delta-V Dilemma is a browser-based space engineering and strategy game that challenges players to design spacecraft capable of completing missions within limited budgets. Players choose from 63 spacecraft components, including engines, fuel tanks, solar panels, batteries, scientific instruments, and structural systems. Every choice influences spacecraft performance, creating meaningful engineering trade-offs.

Players can follow Story Mode, a chain of missions that can take them from Earth to the Moon, Mars, the asteroid belt, and moons of the outer planets, or take on single Challenge missions. Each mission opens with an illustrated cutscene that sets up the problem. Difficulty changes mission budgets and, in Story Mode, the number of hearts and hints. On the hardest settings, players are not explicitly told what to build; they must work it out from the scenario.

The game evaluates whether each design meets its mission’s power, propulsion, structural, communications, and launch requirements. Adding equipment can improve capabilities but also increases mass, power consumption, or cost. Players must balance these interconnected constraints, launch their designs, analyze failures through a flight report, and refine their solutions. Interactive help buttons explain scientific concepts and spacecraft components, making complex engineering principles more accessible.

NASA scientific resources help connect the game’s simplified simulations to real-world space science. JPL Horizons ephemeris data provide reference distances from the Sun, while historical measurements from NASA’s Solar Radiation and Climate Experiment (SORCE) establish a reference sunlight level at Earth’s average orbital distance. Combined through the inverse-square law, these data help calculate solar-panel power for different missions. Mission requirements use simplified orbital mechanics, including vis-viva, Hohmann transfers, and patched-conic approximations, alongside gameplay estimates for some maneuvers and travel times. The game does not run NASA’s General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT). Spacecraft delta-v is calculated using the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation. NASA’s Near-Earth Object Human Space Flight Accessible Targets Study (NHATS) was used to prototype an asteroid survey mission; it is credited in the game’s data panel but is not part of the current playable missions. Hardware performance is simplified for gameplay, and component prices are identified as game estimates rather than actual procurement costs.

The project’s goal is to make space engineering approachable while encouraging systems thinking, critical reasoning, and experimentation. Players learn to identify constraints, compare engineering solutions, and understand how changes to one component can affect an entire spacecraft. Failures provide meaningful feedback and opportunities for improvement. A built-in level editor also allows players to create their own mission scenarios from the game’s illustrations, choose what must be built, and set a budget. Automated validation checks and an optional Claude-powered AI review check whether the story, picture descriptions, destination, and budget make sense together.

Delta-V Dilemma was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with Canvas-based illustrations and animations. Node.js supports development scripts and automated testing, while Vite provides the local development environment. Cloudflare Workers hosts the browser game and can host its optional AI-review endpoint. Claude and OpenAI Codex were used as development assistants.

The project combines spacecraft engineering, scenario-based storytelling, interactive scientific learning, and authentic NASA reference data in a single gameplay experience. Development focused on balancing scientific credibility, intuitive feedback, visual clarity, and engaging gameplay. Delta-V Dilemma aims to help players experience engineering decisions, learn through experimentation, and develop greater confidence in exploring space science and technology.
